sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
LensVLM treats compressed visual context as a reversible representation

Rendering many pages of text into images can shrink a long token sequence, but aggressive downscaling eventually makes characters unreadable. LensVLM separates scanning from reading: it first examines compressed page images, then invokes learned expansion tools only for pages judged relevant. On seven text-QA benchmarks, the authors report accuracy comparable to a full-text upper bound at 4.3× effective compression, with advantages over retrieval and compression baselines extending to 10.1×.

The useful systems idea is not “OCR through a VLM.” It is selective decompression under model control. The compressed representation preserves a global map of the context; expansion is a costly random-access operation. That makes the architecture closer to a memory hierarchy than to ordinary retrieval: scan cheap summaries, identify an address, then fetch the high-fidelity region. The failure mode is also clear—if the coarse view suppresses the clue needed to choose a page, the model never requests the evidence. Training therefore has to make routing robust, not merely make expanded reading accurate. Apple research page

VisHarness trains the generalist to call specialists rather than imitate them

VisHarness keeps a language-capable visual agent responsible for planning and dialogue, while delegating detection, segmentation, counting and other low-level operations to heterogeneous expert models. The agent is trained to choose and sequence those tools over multiple turns. A dynamic visual-memory archive prevents every intermediate mask or annotated image from remaining in the active context and multiplying visual-token cost.

This is a pragmatic alternative to distilling every capability into one model. Specialist vision systems retain their precision and can be replaced independently; the learned component is the policy that turns a natural-language objective into a sequence of measurable operations. The engineering risk moves from raw perception to orchestration: coordinate systems, object identities and uncertainty must remain consistent across tools, or a correct mask from one expert becomes the wrong referent in the next turn. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: LSM-tree compaction is a three-way amplification trade-off
sections.content:
A log-structured merge tree makes writes cheap by appending them to an in-memory sorted table and periodically flushing immutable sorted files to disk. Reads then face the accumulated history: the same key may appear in several files, and deleted values remain as tombstones until background compaction merges runs and discards obsolete versions.

The compaction policy decides which cost the database pays:

  • Leveled compaction keeps roughly one non-overlapping sorted run per level. Reads and space use are good because few runs need checking, but a small incoming run may repeatedly rewrite overlapping data in a much larger level: higher write amplification.
  • Tiered compaction waits for several similarly sized runs and merges them together. Each byte is rewritten less often, but reads may probe more runs and temporary disk use can spike: higher read and space amplification.
  • Hybrids use tiering near the top, where files arrive rapidly, and leveling near the bottom, where most bytes live.

This is why “the database wrote 1 GB” does not mean the SSD received 1 GB. A write-heavy workload, point-lookups, range scans, overwrite skew and available disk headroom imply different compaction choices. Bloom filters and block indexes can reduce read cost, but they do not erase the basic conservation law: less rewriting usually means tolerating more versions or more files somewhere else. RocksDB compaction overview · Universal/tiered compaction

sections.title: Non-CS science: two patient-specific medicines selectively lowered a faulty epilepsy gene
sections.content:
Some severe childhood epilepsies are caused by a gain-of-function SCN2A variant: one copy of the gene makes a sodium channel that is too active, so neurons become easier to fire uncontrollably. Researchers designed a different antisense oligonucleotide, or ASO, for each of two boys aged 9 and 14. An ASO is a short synthetic strand that binds a chosen RNA message and reduces how much protein is made from it.

The difficult part was selectivity. Rather than suppressing both copies of SCN2A, each drug targeted a harmless genetic marker carried on the same chromosome as the disease-causing variant. That let it preferentially reduce the mutant transcript while preserving the healthy copy. Delivered by lumbar injection, the two individualized treatments were associated with seizure-frequency reductions of 26% and 90%, fewer accompanying medicines and improvements in developmental skills; no ASO-related serious adverse events were reported.

This is not yet a general cure. These were two parallel n-of-1 studies, follow-up remains limited, and making a bespoke drug for every variant is expensive and slow. The broader route may be semi-personalized: the researchers found compatible target markers in about 16% of a separate infant cohort, so one allele-selective design could potentially serve multiple patients who share the same marker arrangement. Open-access study

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Iran / Strait of Hormuz: Washington paused a prepared new strike while seeking a rapid agreement covering the strait and Iran’s nuclear programme. The pause reduces immediate escalation risk, but it is conditional diplomacy backed by mobilized force; the relevant test is sustained commercial passage through Hormuz, not the announcement alone. Reuters · AP

  • OPEC+: the core group approved a 188,000-barrel-per-day September quota increase, completing the formal rollback of 1.65 million bpd in voluntary cuts. Actual supply may rise much less because conflict and export disruption already prevent some members from reaching their quotas; the next political fight is the capacity review that will set 2027 baselines and redistribute market share inside the group. Reuters

  • Ukraine: Russia’s 31 July attack used 35 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles, and 185 drones, killing ten people around Kyiv. Ukraine said it intercepted only one ballistic missile because Patriot interceptors were exhausted. The constraint is increasingly industrial and allocative: the same scarce interceptor stock is demanded by several theatres, while cheap drones help saturate the defence before ballistic weapons arrive. Reuters

  • France–United States: a dispute over the renewed term of UN human-rights chief Volker Türk has moved from rhetoric into diplomatic procedure. After the General Assembly approved the extension 144–10 with 13 abstentions, U.S. officials considered delaying France’s proposed ambassador to Washington. Agrément for an ambassador is normally quiet routine; using it as leverage would convert a disagreement over a multilateral appointment into a bilateral personnel veto. Reuters on the UN dispute · Reuters on the ambassador nomination

  • Nigeria–South Africa: after attacks and looting against African migrants, Pretoria promised prosecutions and stronger protection while Abuja compiled compensation claims; roughly 1,490 Nigerians had been repatriated. The bilateral de-escalation matters, but police protection and prosecutions—not softened communiqués—will determine whether anti-migrant groups retain an informal veto over who can live and trade locally. Reuters

sections.title: Marxist fragment
sections.content:
“the motivation of society by unsocial, particular interests”

— Karl Marx, Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844, section on human requirements and the division of labour, Progress Publishers translation. Primary text

Marx is attacking a specific contradiction in political economy. Exchange and division of labour prove that production is thoroughly social: each person depends on the activity of many others. Yet the same theory explains coordination through private owners pursuing separate advantage. Social interdependence appears not as conscious collective organization but as an external market compulsion.

This is more precise than saying that capitalism makes people selfish. The contradiction is institutional: useful cooperation is real, but its direction is mediated by property and exchange, so collectively produced capacities confront producers as somebody else’s asset or as an impersonal price signal. The passage comes from the 1844 Paris manuscripts, before Marx had developed the mature value theory of Capital, but it already isolates the split between social production and private command.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Mary Astell: contractual freedom cannot stop at the household door

“If all Men are born Free, how is it that all Women are born Slaves?”

— Mary Astell, Some Reflections upon Marriage, third edition, 1706. Project Gutenberg text

Astell turns liberal language against a social order that treated marriage as naturally hierarchical. Her point is not that every marriage literally equals chattel slavery, but that a theory grounding legitimate authority in free consent becomes unstable when women are educated for dependence, denied realistic exit and then said to have consented. The friction remains useful: formal choice is weak evidence of freedom when institutions manufacture the available options.

Jeremy Bentham: rights need institutions, not metaphysical adjectives

“Natural rights is simple nonsense … nonsense upon stilts.”

— Jeremy Bentham, Anarchical Fallacies, written 1796. Text excerpt

Bentham’s provocation is that a right without law, enforcement or a specified duty-bearer is not yet an operative right. He feared declarations of “imprescriptible” rights would let each faction treat its preferred moral claim as superior to positive law. The weakness is obvious: if legal recognition is the only source of rights, unjust law cannot violate rights by definition. Modern rights discourse usually keeps Bentham’s institutional demand while rejecting his reduction—moral rights criticize law; legal rights make that criticism enforceable.

sections.title: French usage: **ça m’arrange** versus **ça me va**
sections.content:
Both can translate as “that works for me,” but they answer different questions.

  • Ça me va means I accept that / that suits me. It is comparatively neutral: On se retrouve à 19 h ? — Ça me va. It also describes fit or appearance: Cette veste te va bien.
  • Ça m’arrange means that is convenient or advantageous for me. It foregrounds schedule, effort or interest: Si on décale à jeudi, ça m’arrange. Depending on context, it can sound candidly self-interested: Ça l’arrange de ne rien dire.

In speech, the negative commonly loses ne: Demain matin, ça m’arrange pas trop. Use ça me va for simple agreement; use ça m’arrange when the proposal solves a practical constraint. Larousse, arranger

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content: Three direct, playable recommendations are embedded below. The queue button opens the same three exact videos in sequence.

items.label: Classical
items.piece: Niels Gade — String Octet in F major, Op. 17
items.description: A chamber-music rotation after several orchestral and concertante successes. Gade uses the Mendelssohnian octet model—eight strings behaving sometimes as one brilliant ensemble, sometimes as two choirs—but gives the first movement more weight and the Andantino a broad, uncomplicated lyricism. The likely miss is that its brightness may feel less harmonically saturated than the late-Romantic pieces that scored 9; the test is whether the energetic outer movements still feel developed rather than merely fluent.

items.label: Jazz / fusion
items.description: Japanese fusion with an unusually clear large-scale route: stated theme, keyboard expansion, a bass-and-drums centre section, then an earned return to the main groove. It is considerably more extroverted than the recent European trios, but the solos remain attached to a recognizable architecture. The risk is polished virtuosity tipping into fusion gloss; the payoff is rhythmic detail that remains foreground listening rather than ambience.

items.label: Other
items.piece: Mayra Andrade — Manga — live aux Bouffes du Nord
items.description: Cape Verdean-rooted contemporary pop built from a firm vocal hook, elastic bass and percussion that complicate the pulse without making the song feel busy. It tests a warmer, more rhythmically active vocal lane than the recent Luedji Luna and Lhasa picks, while keeping melodic identity ahead of production texture. The possible miss is that the groove may carry more of the development than the harmony.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: Edo-period geometry problems were displayed as religious offerings
sections.content:
In early-modern Japan, mathematicians and amateurs painted geometry problems and theorems on wooden sangaku tablets and dedicated them at Shinto shrines and Buddhist temples. They were not private notebooks: the tablet publicly displayed a problem, an answer or a compact proof, often with carefully coloured circles and polygons.

The custom flourished during the Edo period, especially from the late seventeenth through nineteenth centuries. Samurai, merchants and farmers participated; rival schools could use a tablet both as an offering and as a challenge to other problem-solvers. The National Diet Library notes that about 1,000 survive, roughly 400 from the Edo period, while the second-oldest surviving example was dedicated at Kyoto’s Yasaka Shrine in 1691.

Sangaku matter because they show mathematics functioning simultaneously as research communication, public competition, visual art and devotional practice. A theorem did not need a journal or university seminar to circulate: it could hang under a shrine roof where travellers and local practitioners encountered it. National Diet Library · Smithsonian Libraries catalogue note

sections.title: Puzzle: Yablo’s paradox without a self-referential sentence
sections.content:
Imagine an infinite list of statements:

  • S₁: Every statement after S₁ is false.
  • S₂: Every statement after S₂ is false.
  • S₃: Every statement after S₃ is false.
  • and so on forever.

No statement mentions itself, and the reference graph has no cycle: each statement points only forward.

Suppose some Sₙ is true. Then every later statement is false, including Sₙ₊₁. But if Sₙ₊₁ is false, it is not true that all statements after it are false—so some still later statement must be true, contradicting Sₙ.

Now suppose every statement is false. Then all statements after S₁ are false, which is exactly what S₁ says; S₁ is therefore true.

Where should the diagnosis fall: classical two-valued truth, the completed infinite list, or the idea that an acyclic but infinitely descending dependency is harmless? A useful constraint is that every finite truncation can be assigned truth values consistently; the contradiction appears only in the unbounded sequence. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy
